```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
```

`ggplotify` converts a plot into a `grob` or a `ggplot` object. Two functions do
the work, `as.grob()` and `as.ggplot()`, and both accept four kinds of input:

- a plot call, written as a formula (`~barplot(1:10)`) or an `expression`
- a function that draws to a graphics device when it is called
- a graphic object produced by another package, such as a `ggplot` or `trellis`
- a plot captured by `grDevices::recordPlot()`

The output is an ordinary `grid` object, so a plot drawn by base graphics can be
arranged, aligned, annotated and inset like a `ggplot2` plot. The classes
`as.grob()` dispatches on are listed at the end of this document.

## Plot calls

```{r}
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplotify)

p1 <- as.grob(~barplot(1:10, main = "formula"))
p2 <- as.grob(expression(barplot(11:20, main = "expression")))
p3 <- as.grob(function() barplot(21:30, main = "function"))
```

`as.grob()` replays the call on a graphics device and captures the result with
`gridGraphics::grid.echo()`. A formula or an expression is evaluated in the
environment `as.grob()` was called from, which is the global environment at the
top level. A variable that is local to the function doing the conversion is
therefore not visible, and needs `envir`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
as.grob(~barplot(n), envir = environment())
```

A function is simply called, which makes it the most general form: any code that
draws to a device works, and it carries its own environment with it.

## Graphic objects

A plot that already exists as an object needs no call to be written for it, and
`as.grob()` takes it directly. Some classes are converted straight from the
object, others are drawn once into a device and captured from there.

```{r}
#| warning: false
library(lattice)

p4 <- as.grob(densityplot(~mpg | cyl, data = mtcars))
p5 <- as.grob(ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point())
```

`p4` is a `trellis` object returned by `lattice` and `p5` is a `ggplot2` plot.
Converting a `ggplot` object gives back the `gtable` built by
`ggplot2::ggplotGrob()`, and a `grob` is returned unchanged.

## Recorded plots

`grDevices::recordPlot()` stores the display list of the current device. On most
file devices that list is not kept unless it is switched on, so
`dev.control(displaylist = "enable")` has to come before the plot is drawn.

```{r}
#| fig.height: 6
#| warning: false
pdf(tempfile(fileext = ".pdf"))
dev.control(displaylist = "enable")
plot(1:10, type = "b", main = "recorded")
recording <- recordPlot()
invisible(dev.off())

as.ggplot(recording)
```

This makes it possible to draw a plot once, keep the recording, and place it in a
composed figure later. A recording of a device whose display list stayed
inhibited holds no graphics, and `as.grob()` says so rather than returning an
empty grob.

```{r}
#| warning: false
pdf(tempfile(fileext = ".pdf"))
plot(1:10)
empty <- recordPlot()
invisible(dev.off())

try(as.grob(empty))
```

Replaying a recording needs the same R version, the same type of graphics device
and the packages that drew the original plot, and it is only guaranteed within
the session that called `recordPlot()`.

## Drawing with grid

A converted plot is a `grob`, so `grid.draw()` renders it and `pushViewport()`
places it inside another plot.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 7
#| warning: false
library(grid)

grid.newpage()
grid.draw(p1)
vp <- viewport(x = .4, y = .72, width = .4, height = .35)
pushViewport(vp)
grid.draw(p2)
upViewport()
```

`grid.draw()` has methods for the three call forms as well, so no conversion is
needed when the only goal is to draw a plot.

```{r}
#| warning: false
grid.draw(~barplot(1:10))
```

## Converting to a ggplot object

`as.ggplot()` puts the converted grob into a `ggplot2` plot with a blank panel
and `theme_void()`. Layers, scales and themes can then be added on top of the
original figure.

```{r}
#| warning: false
as.ggplot(~barplot(1:10)) +
    annotate("text", x = .6, y = .5, label = "Hello base plot",
             size = 6, color = "firebrick", angle = 45) +
    annotate("point", x = .2, y = .8, color = "steelblue", size = 4)
```

`scale`, `hjust` and `vjust` place the original figure in a rectangle, and
`angle` rotates it. The rectangle runs from `1 - scale` to `scale` on both axes
and is shifted by `hjust` and `vjust`, so `scale = 1` fills the panel and
`scale = .9` leaves a tenth of it at every edge. The figure is clipped to that
rectangle rather than shrunk into it, which is why a small `scale` cuts titles
and axis labels off instead of drawing them smaller. In practice `scale` stays
close to 1.

```{r}
#| warning: false
as.ggplot(~barplot(1:10, main = "base plot"), scale = .95, hjust = .05, vjust = .05)
```

`angle` rotates the figure. A rotated figure goes through a viewport rather
than the rectangle above, and `scale` is the width of that viewport.

```{r}
#| warning: false
as.ggplot(~plot(1:10, type = "b", main = "base plot"), angle = 90,
          scale = .6, hjust = -.15)
```

Grid cannot clip to a viewport that is rotated by something other than a
multiple of 90 degrees, so a non-right angle emits the warning
`cannot clip to rotated viewport` once for every clipped grob. The figure is
still drawn.

```{r}
#| warning: false
as.ggplot(~plot(1:10, type = "b", main = "base plot"), angle = 45, scale = .45)
```

A plot drawn by a `grid` based package converts the same way. Capture it with
`grid2grob()` rather than a formula: a formula is replayed by
`gridGraphics::grid.echo()`, which does not understand the grid drawing
operations of the original plot and emits one
`unsupported operation on the graphics display list` warning for every
operation it cannot replay. `vcd::mosaic` here, with a `ggplot2` annotation
added on top of it.

```{r}
library(vcd)
data(Titanic)

as.ggplot(grid2grob(mosaic(Survived ~ Sex, data = as.data.frame(Titanic)))) +
    annotate("label", x = .5, y = .97, label = "converted from vcd",
             size = 4.5, fill = "white")
```

## Arranging plots

`aplot` lays out plots with `patchwork` and calls `as.ggplot()` on any input that
is not a plot object, so base plots can be mixed with `ggplot2` plots without a
conversion step.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 12
#| fig.height: 7
#| warning: false
library(aplot)

plot_list(~barplot(1:10), ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point(),
          ~plot(sin), densityplot(~mpg | cyl, data = mtcars),
          ncol = 2, labels = LETTERS[1:4])
```

A list of already converted grobs can be arranged the same way.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 12
#| fig.height: 4
#| warning: false
plot_list(gglist = list(p1, p2, p3, p5), ncol = 4, widths = c(1, 1, 1, 1.2))
```

Two panels side by side, the same data drawn by the two graphics systems.
`colorspace` provides one palette for both, so the colors match. Joining the two
with `+` is patchwork's doing: loading it registers a `+.gg` method that takes
over from the one in `ggplot2`.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 4.5
#| warning: false
library(colorspace)
library(patchwork)

col <- rainbow_hcl(3)
color <- col[iris$Species]

as.ggplot(~plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width, col = color, pch = 15,
                xlab = "Sepal.Length", ylab = "Sepal.Width",
                main = "base graphics"),
          scale = .9) +
    ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, color = Species)) +
    geom_point(shape = 15) +
    scale_color_manual(values = col, name = "") +
    ggtitle("ggplot2")
```

## Insetting one plot into another

`ggplot2::annotation_custom()` takes a grob and places it at data coordinates,
which is the simplest way to inset a converted plot.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 8
#| warning: false
ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, color = Species)) +
    geom_point() +
    annotation_custom(as.grob(recording), xmin = 6, xmax = 7.8,
                      ymin = 3.3, ymax = 4.4)
```

The inset is clipped to the panel and is positioned in data coordinates. When
the position should instead be relative to the page, `grid.draw()` inside a
`viewport()`, as shown above, does the job.

## Insets and subviews

Every example above ends as an ordinary `grid` object, and that is the point of
the package. A plot drawn by base graphics, a `lattice` panel, a `vcd` diagram
and a captured recording all become the same kind of object, so any package that
can place a grob can place them.

`ggplot2::annotation_custom()` is the simplest case, and the one just shown.
`aplot::insert_left()`, `insert_right()`, `insert_top()` and `insert_bottom()`
attach a second plot as a marginal panel, and a converted plot is a `ggplot`
object, so it goes wherever a `ggplot2` plot goes.

`ggimage::geom_subview()` puts plots inside a panel at data coordinates and
sizes them with `width` and `height`. Its subviews come either from a column of
the data or from the `subview` argument, and each one is converted with
`as.grob()`, so that column may hold a formula, a function, a `ggplot`, a
`trellis` object, a `recordedplot` or a grob. A figure that only base graphics
can draw is then an inset in exactly the same way a `ggplot2` plot is. `ggimage`
re-exports `as.grob()` and `as.ggplot()`, so a user of that package has the
converters attached already.

Worked subview examples are in the `ggimage` documentation and vignette, which is
where the feature is developed. This vignette stops at the conversion.

## Supported input classes

`as.ggplot()` accepts everything `as.grob()` does, since it converts the input
and then wraps it. Methods that belong to another package are looked up when
they are needed, so that package only has to be installed, not loaded.

| Input class | Produced by |
|---|---|
| `formula`, `expression`, `function` | any base graphics code |
| `recordedplot` | `grDevices::recordPlot()` |
| `grob` | `grid` |
| `ggplot` | `ggplot2` |
| `patchwork` | `patchwork` |
| `aplot`, `oncoplot`, `gglist` | `aplot` |
| `trellis` | `lattice` |
| `Heatmap` | `ComplexHeatmap` |
| `pheatmap` | `pheatmap` |
| `eulergram` | `eulerr` |
| `upset` | `UpSetR` |
| `meme` | `meme` |
| `tmap` | `tmap` |
| `bbplot` | `ggbio` |
| `magick-image` | `magick` |

A `gTree` has no method of its own and is handled by the `grob` method, since it
inherits from `grob`.
